title: John and June Allcott Gallery: taylor barnes, Weight of Light
location: Hanes Art Center, John and June Allcott Gallery
description:
Reception and artist conversation: October 29, 2026, 5:00 pm

 

Weight of Light is an exhibition of seven works by multidisciplinary artist taylor barnes, created during her year-long residency at West Orchid in Pine Lake, Georgia. Weight of Light considers the relationship between material, perception, and the ongoing process of becoming. Emerging from a period of experimentation and personal reflection, the works occupy an ambiguous space between painting and object. Neither fixed representations nor resolved compositions, the works function as thresholds—sites of transition where questions of origin, transformation, and self-possession remain open.

 

barnes approaches the canvas as a material structure rather than a passive surface. Through staining, layering, saturation, and the transformation of matter between solid and liquid states, she explores the physical and conceptual possibilities of charcoal. Materials shift, settle, resist, and respond, creating conditions in which chance, absence, and emergence become integral to the work. The works do not seek resolution through conventional notions of completion. Instead, they retain evidence of their making—gestures, interruptions, accumulations, and erasures that reveal the instability and possibility inherent in transformation. What remains visible is a record of decisions, encounters, and material negotiations. The works resist linear narratives of progress, suggesting instead a cyclical understanding of origin, movement, and revelation. Abstract maps, they trace an unfolding relationship between the known and obscured. Darkness and light emerge not as opposing forces, but as interdependent conditions which continually refigure perception and understanding. Black, the central color and philosophical foundation of barnes' practice, becomes a space of depth, presence, and possibility—a means of considering how material holds identity, memory, and lived experience. Informed by bell hooks' writings on objectification and subjectivity, barnes' work engages questions of agency, visibility, and the reclamation of self. Ultimately, Weight of Light proposes ascension not as transcendence or arrival, but as an ongoing practice of self-possession. Through material experimentation and an embrace of uncertainty, barnes creates space for the possibility that becoming is neither linear nor complete, but continually negotiated through acts of making, unmaking, and reclamation.

 

taylor barnes is a multidisciplinary artist working across ceramics, fibers, and drawing. Her practice investigates spirituality, oral history, and structures of power through material and form. Working primarily with clay, fabric, string, and charcoal, she translates emotion and lived experience into material forms that hold traces of labor, memory, and ritual. barnes received her MFA in Fibers from the University of North Texas. She lives and works between Georgia and Austin, Texas.

 

Admission: Free

Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm

 

A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE.

 

Artist website: https://www.barnesartistry.com/ 

 

For more information, please contact: Annette Lawrence, annettel@unc.edu

title: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage
description: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Join us November 13–15, 2026, in Durham, NC for the Griot & Grey Owl Black Southern Writers Conference, a three-day celebration of Black Southern literature, storytelling, culture, and community. 
This year’s theme, “We Were Never Meant to Survive: Rest, Resilience and Radical Joy,” explores how Black writers and communities use storytelling to preserve memory, imagine possibility, reclaim rest, and create joy. title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

title: NHBA Bird Outing
description: Contact Claire Cote at clairemccote@gmail.com with questions. The location will be Mason Farm Biological Preserve in Chapel Hill, located behind the Finley Golf Course at 500 Finley Golf Course Rd., Chapel Hill. Going south on US 15-501, turn left onto Old Mason Farm Rd. at the stop light. After about a mile, turn right at the entrance to Finley and drive around the back of the clubhouse to the parking lot. Drive through the parking lot and continue onto a paved road at the back, right-hand corner of the lot. Follow this road about 100 feet (just past the practice putting green) until you come to a fork in the road and take the right-hand fork onto a gravel road. Go about 0.5 miles until you come to a junction. Turn right to cross a concrete low water crossing across Morgan Creek. Go over the low water crossing and up the embankment to meet in the parking lot. Heavy rains prior to the event may make the low water crossing impassible and result in a location change.This outing is sponsored by the New Hope Bird Alliance (formerly New Hope Audubon).Outings usually last 2-3 hours. No reservations or sign-up needed. If there is a large turnout for any particular outing, we may split into two groups. We do recommend carpooling for families or friend pods; while we love pets, there is a ‘no-pet’ policy for bird outings. New birders and birders of all skill levels are welcome. Please wear long pants, socks, and sturdy shoes (ticks and chiggers may be present). Sun and bug protection are also recommended. Bring snacks and water if you like. Heavy rain will result in cancellation.

title: NCLAFF. UA Wolf Among Swans
location: Smith Warehouse, Ahmadieh Family Lecture Hall, Bay 4, C105
description:
Um Lobo Entre os Cisnes (A Wolf Among Swans). 2025. Dir. Marcos Schechtman, Helena Varvaki (Brazil). 112 min.
Thiago Soares, one of Brazil's greatest ballet dancers, is offering a compelling study of artistic excellence emerging from marginalized communities. Because the mentor-student relationship invites critical discussion about power dynamics, cultural transmission, and the transformative process of artistic formation. And because its cross-cultural narrative-from Rio's favelas to the Royal Ballet in London-provides rich material for examining class mobility, cultural capital, and the globalization of the performing arts. A Wolf Among Swans is a biographical drama that follows the extraordinary journey of Thiago Soares, a boy from the suburbs of Rio de Janeiro who trades the rhythms of hip hop for the discipline of classical ballet.

In this workshop, we’ll learn about the different versions of this ever-popular herb (with lots of copycats), why they aren’t equal and which ones are worthy medicine for your apothecaries. And we’ll dive deep into all of the usual fun stuff -- how it’s harvested, where cinnamon hails from and all the lore and fun facts! [Grab your spot here](www.unityholisticwellnesscenter.org)

title: Living History Museum Days at Hickory Ridge History Museum in Boone, NC
description:
We're going back to our roots.

This season, Hickory Ridge History Museum proudly reintroduces Living History Museum Days, a return to the immersive, hands-on spirit that once defined us as Hickory Ridge Living History Museum and “village”. On select days this summer, the cabins will come alive with the sights, sounds, and smells of 18th-century life in the North Carolina mountains.

From open-hearth cooking and blacksmithing to weaving, spinning, woodworking, and frontier chores, guests will experience a day in the life of the early settlers who called this region home. Our interpreters and volunteers will demonstrate traditional skills throughout the village, inviting you to explore, ask questions, and connect with the everyday stories of Appalachian history.

Whether you’re a longtime visitor or discovering us for the first time, Living History Museum Days are your chance to step deeper into the past and to be part of its future.

Interested in volunteering or learning an 18th-century skill? We’re always looking for new hands to help bring the holler to life. Reach out to learn more about becoming part of SAHA family!

Adult leaders and chaperones may also buy a tour ticket if they’re interested in going on the guided tour of the underground mine. Tour tickets are $5.00 for adults 13 and older.

title: JENNY BLAZING: CAROLINA, OR THEREABOUTS
location: 5 Points Gallery, 109 E Chapel Hill St, Durham, NC, 27701, United States
description:
5 Points Gallery is pleased to present Carolina, or Thereabouts, a new exhibition of mixed-media paintings by Featured Artist Jenny Blazing exploring the shifting nature of place through observation, memory, and imagination. Grounded in Blazing’s experiences of Carolina, the layered works draw from travel, accumulated visual memories, and unexpected connections that emerge as the paintings evolve to create landscapes that feel familiar without belonging to any single geography. Throughout the gallery, visitors can also enjoy work by our ten Triangle-based artists, offering a refreshing mix of painting, sculpture, fused glass, mixed media, and finely crafted furniture, with each artist bringing a distinct creative perspective. Join us for the Opening Reception on Friday, October 16, 2026, from 6–9 pm to meet the artist. Carolina, or Thereabouts runs from October 15 through November 14, 2026. Image: The Sun, The Tree, and Everything Between, acrylic and hand-painted paper on stretched canvas, 36×36 inches. 
Visit 5 Points Gallery in person or online at https://5pointsgallery.com. All work from the exhibition is available for shipping or pickup. Gallery hours: Thursdays and Fridays 5–9pm, Saturdays 1–9pm. Artists are available to talk about their work. For a private viewing, contact us at info@5pointsgallery.com.

title: The 2026 Zeidman Memorial Colloquium: Making Sense of the Midterm Elections
description:
The John Fisher Zeidman Memorial Colloquium on Politics and the Press at Duke University was established by Philip and Nancy Zeidman in memory of their son. John Zeidman, a Duke student, died in 1982 after contracting viral encephalitis while studying in China. The Zeidman Colloquium celebrates John's passion for examining the interaction of politics and the press.

The Zeidman Colloquium is a panel discussion with media experts, produced biennially shortly after U.S. national elections take place.

title: The Comeback of Blue-Throated Macaws
location: Nature Research Center, 121 West Jones Street, Raleigh, NC, 27601, United States
description:
20 years of conservation success: the comeback of blue-throated macaws
 
Join us along with the Wake Audubon Society in the SECU Daily Planet Theater for a special presentation with Dorothy Paterson, executive director for Bird Endowment. 
Ms. Dorothy Paterson, the President & Executive Director of Bird Endowment, will join us via Zoom to deliver “Twenty Years of Conservation Success: The Comeback of Blue-Throated Macaws” inside the SECU Daily Planet Theater. 
Blue-Throated Macaws are a critically endangered parrot native exclusively to the Beni Savannas of north-central Bolivia. Only 300-500 individuals remain in the wild. Their severe decline is driven by habitat loss, the illegal pet trade, and the historic use of its feathers in traditional dances.

description:

Then head outside on a plant walk to learn how to identify woody trees and shrubs by their leaves, bark, flowers, fruit and growing conditions, and learn to spot characteristic clues to determine the plant families to which they belong. Discussion will include common and obscure uses for woody plants that can support overall human health, well-being and sustenance, along with relationships between woody plants and fungi.

title: 10th Annual Liberty Arts Iron Pour
location: Durham Central Park, 501 Foster St, Durham, NC, 27701, United States
description:
Liberty Arts is proud to announce the 10th Annual Iron Pour, taking place on November 14, 2026, from 4-9pm. Register to attend so we know you’ll be there! 
Every November since 2016, Liberty Arts has hosted a FREE public arts event in Durham Central Park. All evening and into the night, thousands of pounds of molten iron will be poured into molds in an exciting fiery display, creating iron tiles designed by the public and sculptures made by NC artists. The event will also feature performances, local food trucks, craft beer, art vendors, and opportunities to learn from and engage with this spectacular art form. The Iron Pour has become a major cultural anchor in Durham, bringing together thousands of people to celebrate fire, metal, and creative expression in a dynamic, interactive setting. 
This year, on the events’ TENTH ANNIVERSARY, Liberty Arts is celebrating 10 years of Pouring with Purpose, sparking creativity and continuing collaboration between artists and community. 
We invite our community to engage with metal casting like you’ve never seen it before, and experience a wide array of art making. Heat and fire come to life through glassblowing, flame working, blacksmithing and more. Participate in unique workshops, forge bonds with community partners, and be dazzled by performing artists. 
As we celebrate our 10th anniversary, remember that the Iron Pour is also Liberty Arts’ largest fundraiser! When you make a small donation, become a local partner, or join us as a distinguished sponsor, you provide direct support to our community initiatives. Your Iron Pour contribution helps sustain programming like IRON HEROES, and collaborations with local non profits and educational institutions. Liberty Arts is committed to providing accessible opportunities for unique art making through our ongoing programming. Consider making a donation when you register to attend! 
The Iron Pour promises to dazzle audiences with its unique blend of art, fire, music, food and Bull City spirit. Witness the mesmerizing process of creating sculptures from molten iron, as skilled artists push the boundaries of this ancient process. 
This year’s event features: 
Glassblowing demonstrations
Blacksmithing demonstrations
Flameworking demonstrations
Woodworking demonstrations
Drumming performances by Batala
Olympic Fencing demonstrations by Forge Fencing
Performance Iron Casting Pieces
Interactive Fire Sculptures & Metal Casting Gallery Exhibit
Make and take crafts with the Scrap Exchange
Delicious eats from local food trucks and vendors
Original artwork and handmade goods from 24+ local artists
Admission is FREE, and ample parking is available. 
Mark your calendars for November 14th and join the festivities in Durham Central Park!

title: Faculty Recital: Gabriel Richard — The Three Bs
description:
Explore three centuries of musical innovation as faculty violinist Gabriel Richard presents "The Three Bs: Bach, Bartók, Boulez-Perspectives on Form from the Baroque to the Contemporary."

The program traces the evolution of musical form through a violin transcription of Bach's BWV 542, Bartók's Sonata for Solo Violin, Boulez's Anthèmes I, and Bach's Partita No. 2 for Solo Violin. Moving from the intricate architecture of the Baroque to the bold musical languages of the 20th century, the recital reveals striking connections among three composers whose works continually challenge and redefine the possibilities of sound.

This event is free and open to the public. All are welcome.

title: Trust Yourself: Making Your Life Story Work for You
description:
Raleigh & Triangle Activities Meetup Group
So you’re on the self-improvement spiritual path, doing your best to join the amazing new future of hope and healing that you know in your heart must be true. You and the world didn’t come this far -- through millions of years of miraculous evolution, natural beauty, and ideal human striving -- only to be trashed by the ignorance and violence of the most unimaginative uninspired individuals. Well, you’re absolutely correct, so don’t worry. The Universe is alive and it loves you, with a divine plan that’s unfolding better than we knew. The realities are already split and we turned a corner, so let’s wave our final goodbyes to those who chose war while we were working on peace. The US mid-terms were just one indicator, as more people wake up daily to their own contribution for 2027 to be the year that everything changes.

The question remains: what to do with your personal story? This is no time for denial and spiritual bypassing. Changing timelines doesn’t mean suddenly forgetting all that happened, nor does forgiveness mean accepting it all so nothing changes. As much as the miracles are indeed coming -- including open contact with higher beings, new levels of psychic guidance, and mass healing awakenings -- the real shift is deeper and more profound still. The very meaning of time and space is forever redefined so that the problems we had never existed. We humans certainly struggled and suffered, but unnecessarily. The true challenge of Earth was never to make paradise, because it was already here. You can’t fix what isn’t broken; you can only start using it properly.

This is the magic of reframing. When you suddenly understand what things really mean and how the Universe is built for success, then reality becomes fun and easy. Including your personal life? Especially your personal life! This is not just a theory; you are the Universe in the focus of you, learning how to be the best you to receive all the resources that you need to thrive. The whole system is interconnected, with every part functioning only as well as every other. Does your heart try to do the job of your lungs to oxygenate the blood? Of course not! But by pumping your blood the best that it can, your heart supplies the lungs that supply the heart and vice versa. The holographic Universe is even more magical than this metaphor can imply, because every consciousness creates its own view of the whole. This means that while you must depend on how others function, you are never at the mercy of their decisions for you. Make your own choices and others will follow. When you change, they change. It’s a mirror.

In effect, your personal lifestyle is your control panel on your own Universe in the multiverse. This may be hard to believe at first because we were taught the false negative beliefs of domination. The biggest baddest people supposedly rule, so our personal histories were filled with abuse. The spiritual path became the busy work of endless healing and forgiving, in the hope that our abusers would learn to join us in a better tomorrow. That fantasy crashed on the rocks of increasingly cruel behavior, as the dominators perfected their dehumanizing systems of narcissistic demagoguery, insatiable exploitation, and genocidal fascism. With the planetary ecosystem on the brink now, we’ve run out of other cheeks to turn. Jesus said the meek would inherit the Earth, but pray tell how and when? And how the hell can we stop reacting to the hells from our own hellish backstories that drag us down in complex PTSD?

For this meetup, be willing to bring both your highest hopes and lowest despairs. We’ll see how the false belief systems are self-perpetuating by telling you exactly the wrong way to think about everything. You failed to change other people or fix the world because you never had to. You have nothing to be ashamed of in your personal life story. True positive beliefs will make you feel excited and empowered to be you, because truly you wanted to be nobody else. You don’t need to change as much as you thought you did, when what changes is the meaning and use of what you’ve already done. You’ll learn to trust yourself as you reinterpret your life story in the universal process, whose 7 archetypal stages move your awareness from eternal spirit to sequential human and back again, for the confidence to create your own reality. We’ll look at the symbols and synchronicities for a brand new predestined future, and conclude with a guided meditation to let our higher self lead us Home faster and better than we thought possible.

Welcome! Our Inner Selves Mastery spiritual support group is free online every Sunday 11am-130pm EDT, with the last 30 minutes for a guided meditation. If you can’t stay you can get the recording. You can signup here for this meeting and visit www.signupISM.com for all events, newsletter, videos, and more.

Best wishes,
Carl Johann Schroeder
Inner Selves Mastery
spiritual teaching and coaching

title: University Worship
description:
Join us in worship that offers stirring preaching, inspiring sacred music, and faithful prayer. Held year-round amid the beautiful, soaring architecture of Duke Chapel, this interdenominational Christian service is characterized by vibrant faith, intellectual depth, diverse cultural expressions, and a welcoming community.

To attend a service, navigate to 125 Science Drive, Durham, NC. Parking is available at that address in the Bryan Center Garage with ADA parking in the adjacent surface lot. Parking in the garage is free on Sunday until 2:00 p.m. when using the standard ticket issued upon entering the garage. Regular attendees of the service are encouraged to receive a pass for free parking on Sunday mornings at the visitor desk inside the Chapel.

Resources for the service:
* Make an offering online: https://chapel.duke.edu/offering
* View an online version of the hymnal here: https://hymnary.org/hymnal/UMH

A national leader in the theological study of the art of preaching, Chapel Dean Luke A. Powery preaches regularly at this service, along with a rotation of other Chapel ministers and renowned guest preachers. The acclaimed Duke Chapel Choir and Chapel organists lead the music, supplemented by student chamber groups, professional instrumentalists, and visiting artists.

Services are streamed live on YouTube and broadcast live on channel 12 of the Duke Hospital TV system and on the radio on 620 AM WDNC. Subscribe to the Duke Chapel Sermons podcast on Spotify or Apple Podcasts. Find an archive of Chapel sermons on our website and a more extensive digital archive in the Duke Chapel Recordings collection on the Duke Libraries website.

For a listing of Christian education offerings held before the service, see the Duke Chapel website calendar.

title: NCJSS Welcomes Federica Francesconi
description:
The North Carolina Jewish Studies Seminar welcomes Federica Francesconi, Associate Professor of History and Director of the Judaic Studies Program at the University at Albany, SUNY. Her research and publications address the social, religious, and cultural aspects of the early modern history of Jews in Italy, focusing on the multifaceted politics and dynamics of ghetto life. She has held fellowships in Europe, Israel, and the United States. She served as Viterbi Visiting Professor in Mediterranean Jewish Studies at the University of California, Los Angeles, and has been a fellow at the Herbert D. Katz Center for Advanced Judaic Studies at the University of Pennsylvania and the Oxford Centre for Hebrew and Jewish Studies.

Her recent book, "Invisible Enlighteners: The Jewish Merchants of Modena, from the Renaissance to the Emancipation" (University of Pennsylvania Press, 2021), is the 2022 Helen and Howard R. Marraro Prize Winner, granted by the American Historical Association and the 2021 National Jewish Books Awards Finalist for the JDC-Herbert Katzki Award for Writing Based on Archival Material. Among her other publications, there are two coedited volumes: "From Catalonia to the Caribbean: The Sephardi Orbit from Medieval to Modern Times" (2018) and "Jewish Women's History from Antiquity to the Present" (2021). The latter is the 2021 National Jewish Books Awards Finalist for the Barbara Dobkin Award in Women Studies.

She is currently at work on a new monograph provisionally titled "The Jewish Home in Early Modern Venice: Cosmopolitan Intimacy, Global Networks, and Diasporic Material Culture." The book explores the Jewish home in Venice during the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries as a multi-religious and multi-ethnic webwork of individuals, communities, and objects in motion. The project has received a 2022-24 Gladys Krieble Delmas Grant and a 2024-25 Memorial Foundation for Jewish Culture Fellowship Grant 2024-2025. In Spring 2025, Dr. Francesconi will be a Berenson Fellow at I Tatti, The Harvard University Center for the Renaissance Studies in Florence.

Dr. Francesconi is interested in working with graduate and undergraduate students on early modern Jewish social and cultural history; Mediterranean studies; European history; gender history and theory; material culture, everyday life, and the built environment.

title: World Day of Remembrance for Road Traffic Victims 2026
description:
World Day of Remembrance for Road Traffic Victims – Durham 
Date: Sunday, November 15, 2026 
Time: 4:00 PM – 5:00 PM 
Location: CCB Plaza (201 Corcoran St, Durham, NC) 
Join us at CCB Plaza as we gather to observe the World Day of Remembrance for Road Traffic Victims (WDoR) a global day dedicated to honoring the millions of lives lost or altered by traffic crashes, supporting affected families, and advocating for safer streets in our community. 
Event Highlights
Featured Speaker: Hear from Rich Davis, father of Iazias Davis, who was tragically struck and killed nearly one year ago. Rich will share Iazias’s story and reflect on the deep impact of traffic violence on families and loved ones.
Memorial Reading & Candlelight Vigil: Honoring local lives lost and impacted on Durham’s roads.
Call to Action for Safe Streets: We will speak on local initiatives, infrastructure improvements, and safe-speed policies to eliminate traffic fatalities across Durham.
Moment of Silence: A quiet tribute standing together as a community alongside supporters nationwide.
Who Should Attend?
This gathering is open to everyone—grieving family members, crash survivors, safe streets advocates, first responders, and all community members who want to honor those we’ve lost and push for safer streets in Durham. 
How to Participate
Bring a Tribute: You are welcome to bring a photo, LED candle, or personal memorial item to place at the tribute space.
Spread the Word: Invite friends, neighbors, and colleagues to join us at CCB Plaza.
Together, we remember, support, and act to ensure no more lives are lost on our streets.

Gama Rays. Dir. J.J. Ortiz, Gia Jiménez Huamán. 2026. Colombia. 15 min. Kagaba, with English subtitles.
The softer voice of Saga María, a female Indigenous philosopher, shares the embodied knowledge and practice of transforming natural fibers into Kogi archives. A rare moment with one of the most traditional Indigenous peoples of the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, and probably the most sustainable people on earth. 

For the Indigenous Peoples of the Sierra Nevada de Gonawindúa, known in Spanish as the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta in the north of Colombia, weaving the traditional mochila (GAMA/backpack) represents the act of creating the world, of recreating life; as such, this is the work of the Indigenous women.

This short is produced by P'alante Producciones, DukeEngage Colombia, and the Teyku Community of Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta.

Produced by Miguel Rojas Sotelo.


With the presence of the filmmakers



Chatinos hoy y siempre / NeqA TnyaE NiC QoE SaA TykwiE. 2026. Dir. Gabriela Badillo. 68 Voces 68 Corazones  (MX/USA). Animation.  Chatino with English subtitles. 4 min
A manifesto of the resilience of the Chatino communities in Oaxaca and their diasporas in Durham, North Carolina. By living, working, and embodying their language, Chatinos survive the multiple waves of oppression, coloniality, fear, and displacement. An ode to their culture and traditions, yesterday, today, and forever.

This is the latest animation, number forty-three of sixty-eight stories that rescue and share Mexico's linguistic and cultural diversity. 

*With the presence of the filmmaker and members of the Chatino Community of Durham.

title: John and June Allcott Gallery: taylor barnes, Weight of Light
location: Hanes Art Center, John and June Allcott Gallery
description:
Reception and artist conversation: October 29, 2026, 5:00 pm

 

Weight of Light is an exhibition of seven works by multidisciplinary artist taylor barnes, created during her year-long residency at West Orchid in Pine Lake, Georgia. Weight of Light considers the relationship between material, perception, and the ongoing process of becoming. Emerging from a period of experimentation and personal reflection, the works occupy an ambiguous space between painting and object. Neither fixed representations nor resolved compositions, the works function as thresholds—sites of transition where questions of origin, transformation, and self-possession remain open.

 

barnes approaches the canvas as a material structure rather than a passive surface. Through staining, layering, saturation, and the transformation of matter between solid and liquid states, she explores the physical and conceptual possibilities of charcoal. Materials shift, settle, resist, and respond, creating conditions in which chance, absence, and emergence become integral to the work. The works do not seek resolution through conventional notions of completion. Instead, they retain evidence of their making—gestures, interruptions, accumulations, and erasures that reveal the instability and possibility inherent in transformation. What remains visible is a record of decisions, encounters, and material negotiations. The works resist linear narratives of progress, suggesting instead a cyclical understanding of origin, movement, and revelation. Abstract maps, they trace an unfolding relationship between the known and obscured. Darkness and light emerge not as opposing forces, but as interdependent conditions which continually refigure perception and understanding. Black, the central color and philosophical foundation of barnes' practice, becomes a space of depth, presence, and possibility—a means of considering how material holds identity, memory, and lived experience. Informed by bell hooks' writings on objectification and subjectivity, barnes' work engages questions of agency, visibility, and the reclamation of self. Ultimately, Weight of Light proposes ascension not as transcendence or arrival, but as an ongoing practice of self-possession. Through material experimentation and an embrace of uncertainty, barnes creates space for the possibility that becoming is neither linear nor complete, but continually negotiated through acts of making, unmaking, and reclamation.

 

taylor barnes is a multidisciplinary artist working across ceramics, fibers, and drawing. Her practice investigates spirituality, oral history, and structures of power through material and form. Working primarily with clay, fabric, string, and charcoal, she translates emotion and lived experience into material forms that hold traces of labor, memory, and ritual. barnes received her MFA in Fibers from the University of North Texas. title: Conversation Series - Tess-Brown Lavoie and Professor Allison Neal
description:
Duke English invites you to join us for the first installment of our new Conversation Series. Professor Allison Neal and Duke English PhD candidate Tess-Brown Lavoie will discuss Professor Neal's teaching and her book, American Poetic Voice in the Era of Global Broadcast: Mass Vernacular (2026). Hear her thoughts on how 20th-century sound technologies and mass media shaped American poetic voice.

Book Description:

American Poetic Voice in the Era of Global Broadcast situates American poetry within global media to reveal the broad institutional, technological, and cultural resonances of poetic voice. Reading works by Marianne Moore, W.H. Auden, Frank O'Hara, Adrienne Rich, and Audre Lorde, it traces how poetry intersects with specific sound technologies like the phonograph, telephone, radio, and tape recorder, and various vocal practices and institutions, including elocution instruction, poetry reading circuits, and radio-based cultural diplomacy.

Forging a representative American poetic voice long posed a conceptual obstacle in a country of competing accents and languages. New twentieth-century sound technologies and vocal institutions produced an American voice through mass circulation. American English shifted from the heterogeneous, spoken counterpart of standardized, literary British English to a globally heard network standard. This synthetic American voice sparked a parallel American poetic voice, also mediated through technology and global networks. Routing their poetry through modern communication circuits, American poets created a paradoxically intimate, global "mass vernacular," envisioning lyric voices circulating like other official and mass voices. In this context, the formal poetic elements we associate with the lyric-not just voice but also tone, apostrophe, address, and prosopopoeia-reveal a complex history of American cultural consolidation and global distribution. By bridging the figurative and material dimensions of voice, this book highlights the competing cultural currents underlying lyric address in an age of global English.

title: CEE Seminar - Bacterial biofilms, pigments and javelins
description:
Bacteria often grow in biofilms, cell clusters held together by a self-produced matrix. This lifestyle promotes physiological differentiation, making it difficult to control bacterial growth. My group studies the multicellular physiology of Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a metabolically versatile bacterium that produces diverse virulence factors and is a major cause of biofilm-based infections. To visualize and investigate mechanisms underpinning differentiation in biofilms, we use fluorescent reporters and deuterium labeling paired with microscopy of thin sections and live samples.
We have shown that biofilm subpopulations employ distinct strategies, such as using oxygen-scavenging complexes and endogenous electron-shuttling compounds called phenazines, to sustain metabolic activity. We also observed that such metabolic differentiation correlates with increased drug tolerance. Moreover, our characterization of P. aeruginosa biofilms revealed a virulence factor called the "refractile body" (R-body) - a nanomachine that extends into a spear, likely damaging host cells from within. R-body production is stochastic within biofilms, consistent with the idea that R-body producers disable phagocytes and thereby protect their kin from engulfment.
Overall, our work provides insights into the communal lifestyle of bacteria and informs efforts to control biofilm growth in contexts relevant to human health and society.

title: Genome Dynamics in the Fungal Kingdom
description: The lab of Daniel Croll wants to understand how pathogens evolve to cause disease. For this, we focus mainly on major crop pathogens and investigate mechanisms of rapid adaptation. We are interested in how host resistance mechanisms are circumvented, how pesticides become ineffective, and how pathogens are able to cope with climate challenges. We take a broad view in our work and have strong interests in processes of genome evolution at all levels, from transposable element dynamics to broad species comparisons. We combine computational work with empirical analyses from the field to the bench.

title: 250th Anniversary Celebration of Statia Day
description:
On 13 October 1775, the Continental Congress authorized the purchase of the merchant brigantine Defiance. The ship was acquired in mid-November and moored in Wharton and Humphreys shipyard in Philadelphia where she was converted into a warship through hull strengthening, re-rigging, and ordnance and provisioning at a cost of 300-pound sterling. She was named Andrew Doria after the 16th-century Genoese admiral Andrea Doria. 

The Andrew Doria was a 14-gun Brigantine of the Continental Navy. She is most famous for her participation in the Battle of Nassau—the first amphibious engagement by the Continental Navy and the Continental Marines—and for being the first United States vessel to receive a salute from a foreign power.

Under the command of Captain Isaiah Robinson, the Andrew Doria sailed down the Delaware River on 17 October 1776, for a voyage to the West Indies to obtain a cargo of munitions and military supplies at the Dutch island of Sint Eustatius. The Dutch sovereign island of Sint Eustatius sold arms and ammunition to anyone willing to pay, and it was therefore one of the few places from which the young United States could obtain military stores. The good relationship between St. Eustatius and the United States resulted in the noted "First Salute".

 

On 16 November 1776, the 14-gun American brig Andrew Doria commanded by Captain Isaiah Robinson sailed, flying the Continental Colors of the fledgling United States, into the anchorage below St. Eustatius's Fort Oranje (pronounced “Orange”). Robinson announced his arrival by firing a thirteen-gun salute, one gun for each of the thirteen American colonies in rebellion against Britain. Governor Johannes de Graaff replied with an eleven-gun salute from the cannons of Fort Oranje (international protocol required two guns fewer to acknowledge a sovereign flag). It was the first international acknowledgment of American independence. She was carrying a copy of the Declaration of Independence which was presented to Governor De Graaff. The "first salute" was widely reported in the United States at the time, and later provided the title for Barbara Tuchman's 1988 book, The First Salute: A View of the American Revolution.

President Franklin D. Roosevelt visited St. Eustatius for two hours on 27 February 1939 on USS Houston to recognize the importance of the 1776 "First Salute". He presented a large brass plaque to St. Eustatius, displayed today under a flagpole atop the walls of Fort Oranje, reading:

 

“In commemoration to the salute to the flag of the United States, Fired in this fort November 16. 1776, By order of Johannes de Graaff, Governor of Saint Eustatius, In reply to a National Gun-Salute, Fired by the United States Brig of War Andrew Doria, Under Captain Isaiah Robinson of the Continental Navy, Here the sovereignty of the United States of America was first formally acknowledged to a national vessel by a foreign official.”

Presented by Franklin Delano Roosevelt, President of the United States of America

 

Today, Citizens of St. Eustatius affectionately refer to their island as “Statia” and celebrate Statia Day as a national holiday in celebration of being the first to salute the new nation of the United States of America.

description:
Anna Murray Douglass was a freedom-fighter, strategist, and revolutionary whose contributions have too often been overshadowed by those of her husband, Frederick Douglass. Join author Celeste-Marie Bernier with director, writer, producer, and Duke alumnus Charles Randolph-Wright ("American Prophet: Frederick Douglass in His Own Words"), and Douglass family member Kenneth B. Morris, Jr., for a conversation about "Anna Murray Douglass: Biography of a Revolutionary" (Duke University Press, 2026) the first standalone biography devoted to her life and work.

Drawing on more than thirty years of archival research and collaboration with family descendants, Bernier reveals Anna Murray Douglass's leadership in the struggle against slavery, racism, and white supremacy-from helping secure Frederick Douglass's self-liberation to making the family's homes centers of Underground Railroad activity. The book challenges familiar accounts of individual heroism to illuminate a family's multigenerational commitment to freedom.

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: John and June Allcott Gallery: taylor barnes, Weight of Light
location: Hanes Art Center, John and June Allcott Gallery
description:
Reception and artist conversation: October 29, 2026, 5:00 pm

 

Weight of Light is an exhibition of seven works by multidisciplinary artist taylor barnes, created during her year-long residency at West Orchid in Pine Lake, Georgia. Weight of Light considers the relationship between material, perception, and the ongoing process of becoming. Emerging from a period of experimentation and personal reflection, the works occupy an ambiguous space between painting and object. Neither fixed representations nor resolved compositions, the works function as thresholds—sites of transition where questions of origin, transformation, and self-possession remain open.

 

barnes approaches the canvas as a material structure rather than a passive surface. Through staining, layering, saturation, and the transformation of matter between solid and liquid states, she explores the physical and conceptual possibilities of charcoal. Materials shift, settle, resist, and respond, creating conditions in which chance, absence, and emergence become integral to the work. The works do not seek resolution through conventional notions of completion. Instead, they retain evidence of their making—gestures, interruptions, accumulations, and erasures that reveal the instability and possibility inherent in transformation. What remains visible is a record of decisions, encounters, and material negotiations. The works resist linear narratives of progress, suggesting instead a cyclical understanding of origin, movement, and revelation. Abstract maps, they trace an unfolding relationship between the known and obscured. Darkness and light emerge not as opposing forces, but as interdependent conditions which continually refigure perception and understanding. Black, the central color and philosophical foundation of barnes' practice, becomes a space of depth, presence, and possibility—a means of considering how material holds identity, memory, and lived experience. Informed by bell hooks' writings on objectification and subjectivity, barnes' work engages questions of agency, visibility, and the reclamation of self. Ultimately, Weight of Light proposes ascension not as transcendence or arrival, but as an ongoing practice of self-possession. Through material experimentation and an embrace of uncertainty, barnes creates space for the possibility that becoming is neither linear nor complete, but continually negotiated through acts of making, unmaking, and reclamation.

 

taylor barnes is a multidisciplinary artist working across ceramics, fibers, and drawing. Her practice investigates spirituality, oral history, and structures of power through material and form. Working primarily with clay, fabric, string, and charcoal, she translates emotion and lived experience into material forms that hold traces of labor, memory, and ritual. barnes received her MFA in Fibers from the University of North Texas. She lives and works between Georgia and Austin, Texas.

 

Admission: Free

Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm

 

A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE.

 

Artist website: https://www.barnesartistry.com/ 

 

For more information, please contact: Annette Lawrence, annettel@unc.edu 

 

Image credit: Courtesy of the artist

title: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage
description: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.

title: Stevens Creek Habitat Workday (Waynesville)
description:
Southern Appalachian Highlands Conservancy’s Stevens Creek property is situated on the Eastern edge of the Great Smoky Mountains National Park near the Cataloochee Valley. The Steven’s Creek property serves as an important wildlife corridor for the movement of numerous species headed north and south between Cataloochee and I-40, as well as important habitat for the growing elk population. 
Join NCWF’s Smoky Mountains Wilderness Watch Chapter alongside Southern Appalachian Highlands Conservancy for a habitat workday at Stevens Creek. We will focus the workday on managing open areas by removing tulip poplar saplings to encourage a wider variety of plant species and improve foraging habitat for elk and other wildlife.

title: The Story of Stone in the Culberson Asiatic Arboretum
location: Duke Gardens–Barnes Welcome Center, 420 Anderson Street, Durham, NC, 27705, United States
description:
Join Paul Jones, founding curator of the Culberson Asiatic Arboretum, for a walking tour of some of the most iconic stone features found in the arboretum. You’ll hear the stories behind the stone, including traditional stone lanterns, pathways, waterfalls and lichen-covered boulders that blend seamlessly into the landscape. Hear why specific boulders were chosen and how they were placed, and learn more about the design intent. You’ll discover how a single carefully positioned rock can anchor an entire landscape, and how the interplay of stone, water and plants creates a sense of harmony that feels both timeless and deeply intentional. 
Fee: $22; free for Duke Gardens members with discount code. 
Parking: Parking fees apply.
 
Location: Meet at the Barnes Welcome Center.
 
Accessibility: This will be a small group program that takes place outdoors, traveling on a combination of paved and unpaved paths with some uneven surfaces and moderate inclines.

title: Biomimicry: Nature as a Mentor
location: Swift Creek Bluffs Nature Preserve, 7800 Holly Springs Rd, Raleigh, NC, 27606, United States
description:
Learn about biomimicry at Swift Creek Bluffs!
Biomimicry (from the Greek bios, meaning life, and mimesis, meaning to imitate) is the practice of looking at how plants, animals, and ecosystems solve problems and then copying those designs to solve human challenges. It’s not about using nature as a resource (like cutting down trees for wood); it’s about learning from nature as a mentor. 

Join Hike Leader, Leigh Aultman, for an afternoon of Biological Storytelling. We will walk the short creek loop trail with up to six stops where stories will be shared about local organisms' biological adaptations and how those adaptations and innovations can inform human designs.  This is a free event, but preregistration is required. Due to the size of the parking lot, we will keep the hiking group small and ask that you register by vehicle rather than individual. Feel free to bring guests but please carpool to ensure we have enough space in the parking lot.

title: *IN-PERSON* SF/F Group
description:
Durham Writers Group
We will be at the People's Solidarity Hub at 1805 Chapel Hill Rd, Durham (the teal building). This venue does not serve food or drink, but feel free to bring your own. There is a kitchenette for our use, but be sure to clean up afterwards. The space might be a little cozy; please consider masking or staying home if you have a respiratory ailment.

This sub-group focuses on Speculative Fiction, including Science Fiction, Fantasy and Horror. If you have anything that falls under that category — be it short story, poem, novel-in-progress or screenplay — then come! We'd love to hear from you.

Our format allows each reader 15 minutes to present their work aloud, followed by approximately 20 minutes of feedback from the other attendees. To ensure fairness, each attendee is limited to 1 minute of Initial Feedback time. During that period, the author remains silent. Next, we have a 5 minute Free-For-All discussion about the work -- then the author may speak. (We usually get through three readers.)

Though not required, in order to receive more in-depth feed-back, readers may post their work in advance on our Google Group:
https://groups.google.com/d/forum/durham-sff-writers-group

We ask that participants keep their comments constructive and respectful, focusing on what works or doesn't work in the piece.

We also ask that readers provide a warning, both on the Google Group and during the meeting, if their story features content that some readers might find upsetting. This includes descriptions of violence or sexual content.

Readers are:
• Rob
• Jordan
• Daniel

Backup Readers are:
• Heather

Deep Backup:

***We meet every Tuesday at the same time, but alternate between In-Person*** ***and on Zoom. Members may attend both formats, if desired, but readers will be listed separately under the In-Person or Zoom weeks.***

title: 2026 Stone Memorial Lecture by Alexis Pauline Gumbs
location: The Sonja Haynes Stone Center for Research in Black Culture and History, Stone Center Auditorium
description:
Lecture Title: A Homemade Field of Love: Expansive Understandings of Growth in Times of Change


Description: Community cherished Black feminist writer and scholar Alexis Pauline Gumbs will lead an interactive lecture inspired by the “field” as a form of life, from a field of collard greens, to the quantum field. These mediations on “the field” are inspired by her research on June Jordan, Fannie Lou Hamer, George Washington Carver and her most recent book Primary: After and With Alma Thomas. And what fertilizes it all is the legacy of Sonja Haynes Stone whom this lecture celebrates as a founder of the infinitely possible field of Black Studies.

 

Dr. Alexis Pauline Gumbs is a Queer Black Feminist Love Evangelist and an aspirational favorite cousin to all life. Her work in this lifetime is to facilitate infinite, unstoppable ancestral love in practice. Alexis’ books are portable textual ceremonies. Her most recent book Survival is a Promise: The Eternal Life of Audre Lorde revolutionizes the scale of life writing. Her award-winning meditation Undrowned: Black Feminist Lessons from Marine Mammals offers the critical interspecies love song we need at this urgent stage of our collective evolution. Alexis is also currently working her next book in honor of June Jordan and Fannie Lou Hamer, A Homemade Field of Love (forthcoming from Yale University Press). Alexis is currently a Monument Lab Fellow and a Loss and Damage Collaborative Commissioned Author creating ceremony in honor of the wisdom of climate catastrophe survivors in the legacy of Audre Lorde. Alexis received a 2023 Windham Campbell Prize Winner in Poetry, 2022 Whiting Award in Nonfiction and a 2022 National Endowment for the Arts Fellowship in Prose. Alexis was also a 2020-2021 National Humanities Center Fellow. She has transformed the scope of intellectual, creative and oracular writing with her triptych of experimental works published by Duke University Press (Spill: Scenes of Black Feminist Fugitivity in 2016, M Archive: After the End of the World in 2018 and Dub: Finding Ceremony in 2020.) Unlike most academic texts, Alexis’s work has inspired artists across form to create dance works, installation work, paintings, processionals, divination practices, operas, quilts and more.

 

Read more about the speaker: www.alexispauline.com

Register now: https://go.unc.edu/StoneMemorialLecture

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: John and June Allcott Gallery: taylor barnes, Weight of Light
location: Hanes Art Center, John and June Allcott Gallery
description:
Reception and artist conversation: October 29, 2026, 5:00 pm

 

Weight of Light is an exhibition of seven works by multidisciplinary artist taylor barnes, created during her year-long residency at West Orchid in Pine Lake, Georgia. Weight of Light considers the relationship between material, perception, and the ongoing process of becoming. Emerging from a period of experimentation and personal reflection, the works occupy an ambiguous space between painting and object. Neither fixed representations nor resolved compositions, the works function as thresholds—sites of transition where questions of origin, transformation, and self-possession remain open.

 

barnes approaches the canvas as a material structure rather than a passive surface. Through staining, layering, saturation, and the transformation of matter between solid and liquid states, she explores the physical and conceptual possibilities of charcoal. Materials shift, settle, resist, and respond, creating conditions in which chance, absence, and emergence become integral to the work. The works do not seek resolution through conventional notions of completion. Instead, they retain evidence of their making—gestures, interruptions, accumulations, and erasures that reveal the instability and possibility inherent in transformation. What remains visible is a record of decisions, encounters, and material negotiations. The works resist linear narratives of progress, suggesting instead a cyclical understanding of origin, movement, and revelation. Abstract maps, they trace an unfolding relationship between the known and obscured. Darkness and light emerge not as opposing forces, but as interdependent conditions which continually refigure perception and understanding. Black, the central color and philosophical foundation of barnes' practice, becomes a space of depth, presence, and possibility—a means of considering how material holds identity, memory, and lived experience. Informed by bell hooks' writings on objectification and subjectivity, barnes' work engages questions of agency, visibility, and the reclamation of self. Ultimately, Weight of Light proposes ascension not as transcendence or arrival, but as an ongoing practice of self-possession. Through material experimentation and an embrace of uncertainty, barnes creates space for the possibility that becoming is neither linear nor complete, but continually negotiated through acts of making, unmaking, and reclamation.

 

taylor barnes is a multidisciplinary artist working across ceramics, fibers, and drawing. Her practice investigates spirituality, oral history, and structures of power through material and form. Working primarily with clay, fabric, string, and charcoal, she translates emotion and lived experience into material forms that hold traces of labor, memory, and ritual. barnes received her MFA in Fibers from the University of North Texas. She lives and works between Georgia and Austin, Texas.

 

Admission: Free

Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm

 

A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE.

 

Artist website: https://www.barnesartistry.com/ 

 

For more information, please contact: Annette Lawrence, annettel@unc.edu

title: Methods for Navigating the U.S. Health and Social Sciences Job Market
description:
Knowing how to competitively differentiate oneself to obtain a new job in the U.S. health and social sciences field is important, but not always easy to figure out. This short course provides students with practical tips and insights on how to competitively apply for public health professional jobs in the U.S. relating to research, practice, or policy. The course also focuses on U.S. jobs in the social sciences. There will be four modules. In the 1st module, students will learn about best practices for writing cover letters and curriculum vitae (CVs), preparing for interviews, following up on interviews, integrating non-traditional work and volunteer experiences on one’s CV, integrating coursework skills, and negotiating salaries within a human resource lens. As part of this module, students will also learn about how some health and social sciences positions are funded in order to understand how best to respond to active job postings or how best to pursue job opportunities within professional networks. In the 2nd module, students will review strengths and recommendations for improving a selected set of anonymous CVs. As part of this exercise, students will have the option of submitting their CV one week prior to the short course for the instructor to anonymize, including removing identifying information such as name and contact information. With each student’s prior permission, the instructor and class will share during the short course what they understood and did not understand about the anonymized CV, including suggestions for how to enhance the CV. This is a rare opportunity to hear firsthand how other professionals consume your CV and find out what they deemed to be the most and least valuable components. After the discussion, the CV holder will have the option of revealing themself (or not) to query the instructor and course peers regarding any additional insights. In the 3rd module, students will learn about contemporary approaches to marketing oneself when applying for jobs, including the potential advantages of leveraging personal webpages, professional network sites, conference meetings, business cards, referrals, informational interviews, or social media. We will also discuss several do’s and don’ts. In the final module, students will learn about ways to stay organized and motivated during a job search, including developing a plan relating to the number and type of job positions to apply to and how to fill in possible gaps in one’s CV. This course is designed to provide new knowledge for both students and professionals who are recent graduates of Master’s or doctoral degree programs in health and social sciences.

title: Emotional Eating: The Connection Between Mood & Food
description:
The population of the United States is becoming increasingly obese with each passing decade. There are many speculations about the cause of this phenomenon from an increasing sedentary lifestyle, the ready availability of high caloric foods to stress and even sleep deprivation. However, if people ate only when they were truly hungry and stopped when they were full, there would be no obesity epidemic. This workshop will address the relationship between emotions and food consumption and how to retrain your body and mind to recognize the cues of hunger and to eat for physiological and not emotional reasons.

title: Foreign Policy at the AI Frontier: How AI is Reshaping Progress, Power, and Peace
location: FedEx Global Education Center, Nelson Mandela Auditorium (GEC 1015)
description:
Join the Duke-UNC Rotary Peace Center on Wednesday, November 18 at the FedEx Global Education Center for the launch of Branka Panic's new book, Foreign Policy at the AI Frontier: How AI is Reshaping Progress, Power, and Peace - a comprehensive guide for anyone navigating AI's transformative impact on diplomacy and foreign policy.

 

Organized around three themes, the book traces how Progress and Power are being reshaped by geopolitical competition, the rise of Big Tech as quasi-sovereign actors, and threats from lethal autonomous systems to AI-driven cyber warfare — before turning to Peace, with real-world applications of AI in diplomacy, peacebuilding, and crisis management, and the Global South's growing role in shaping AI's future. Blending case studies with ethical reflection, it closes not with predictions but with aspirations: how nations might navigate AI rivalry and redirect these technologies toward peace.

 

This is not a book about tomorrow; it's about preparing for tomorrow by understanding the choices we make today. Whether you're a diplomat, a technologist, a student, or a citizen navigating a changing world, join us for a conversation about shaping - not merely inheriting - an AI-transformed world.

 

This talk will be held in Nelson Mandela Auditorium at 5:30pm. Free food will be provided. UNC students can register and receive CLE credit by signing up at https://heellife.unc.edu/event/12950032.

title: Ballet BC Medhi Walerski, artistic director
description:
Ballet BC transforms a theater full of strangers into a single, collective audience response—a gasp, a silence, a moment of awe.

 

This triple bill explores what it means to be human in relationship to one another, moving from the vulnerable to the virtuosic, exploring deeply personal stories and moments of quiet intimacy to the exhilaration of masses of bodies moving together as one. 

 

The evening opens with Obsidian by choreographic collaborators Bobbi Jene Smith and Or Schraiber, whose work has been described as “wild and rebellious.” Artistic Director Medhi Walerski’s SWAY follows, inspired by Emily Dickinson’s poem “Hope is the thing with feathers” and set to an original score by Adrien Cronet, creating moments as fleeting and precarious as the hope described in the poem. The evening concludes with Shahar Binyamini’s BOLERO X, set to Ravel’s Boléro, that builds with pulsating drive and excitement as the ranks of Ballet BC dancers multiply their forces, turning the stage into a sweeping, euphoric, collective—and culminating in a finale so extraordinary that a room full of strangers can’t help but respond together.

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: John and June Allcott Gallery: taylor barnes, Weight of Light
location: Hanes Art Center, John and June Allcott Gallery
description:
Reception and artist conversation: October 29, 2026, 5:00 pm

 

Weight of Light is an exhibition of seven works by multidisciplinary artist taylor barnes, created during her year-long residency at West Orchid in Pine Lake, Georgia. Weight of Light considers the relationship between material, perception, and the ongoing process of becoming. Emerging from a period of experimentation and personal reflection, the works occupy an ambiguous space between painting and object. Neither fixed representations nor resolved compositions, the works function as thresholds—sites of transition where questions of origin, transformation, and self-possession remain open.

 

barnes approaches the canvas as a material structure rather than a passive surface. Through staining, layering, saturation, and the transformation of matter between solid and liquid states, she explores the physical and conceptual possibilities of charcoal. Materials shift, settle, resist, and respond, creating conditions in which chance, absence, and emergence become integral to the work. The works do not seek resolution through conventional notions of completion. Instead, they retain evidence of their making—gestures, interruptions, accumulations, and erasures that reveal the instability and possibility inherent in transformation. What remains visible is a record of decisions, encounters, and material negotiations. The works resist linear narratives of progress, suggesting instead a cyclical understanding of origin, movement, and revelation. Abstract maps, they trace an unfolding relationship between the known and obscured. Darkness and light emerge not as opposing forces, but as interdependent conditions which continually refigure perception and understanding. Black, the central color and philosophical foundation of barnes' practice, becomes a space of depth, presence, and possibility—a means of considering how material holds identity, memory, and lived experience. Informed by bell hooks' writings on objectification and subjectivity, barnes' work engages questions of agency, visibility, and the reclamation of self. Ultimately, Weight of Light proposes ascension not as transcendence or arrival, but as an ongoing practice of self-possession. Through material experimentation and an embrace of uncertainty, barnes creates space for the possibility that becoming is neither linear nor complete, but continually negotiated through acts of making, unmaking, and reclamation.

 

taylor barnes is a multidisciplinary artist working across ceramics, fibers, and drawing. Her practice investigates spirituality, oral history, and structures of power through material and form. Working primarily with clay, fabric, string, and charcoal, she translates emotion and lived experience into material forms that hold traces of labor, memory, and ritual. barnes received her MFA in Fibers from the University of North Texas. She lives and works between Georgia and Austin, Texas.

 

Admission: Free

Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm

 

A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE.

 

Artist website: https://www.barnesartistry.com/ 

 

For more information, please contact: Annette Lawrence, annettel@unc.edu

title: Nov 19 - Visualizing and Debugging Hugging Face's LeRobot Data
description:
Raleigh AI, Machine Learning and Computer Vision Meetup
This workshop is a hands-on tour of what actually breaks when you load real LeRobot datasets, and how Voxel51's native LeRobot support in FiftyOne catches it.

**Date, Time and Location**

Nov 19, 2026
9:00 AM - 10:00 AM PST
Online. **[Register for the Zoom!](https://voxel51.com/events/lerobot-workshop-november-19-2026)**

Robot learning data doesn't look like the data that trains most vision-language models. It's temporal, low-dimensional in the parts that matter most, embodiment-specific, and expensive to collect, and increasingly, it's shipped in Hugging Face's LeRobot format. But packaging robot data consistently isn't the same as being able to see it: episodes hide broken metadata, silently dropped sensor modalities, and mismatched schemas between robots that look identical on paper.

Starting from the core differences that make robot data hard (temporal structure, proprioception, action grounding, embodiment heterogeneity, data scarcity), we'll move into live debugging: a metadata bug that broke multiple dataset imports, sensor streams that vanish without an error, and two robots running an identical benchmark whose data is structurally incompatible. By the end, you'll know what to check before you trust a LeRobot dataset, and how to actually look inside one.
source: Meetup: Raleigh AI, ML & Computer Vision

title: Enterprise AI in the Physical World: Navigating the Supply Chain
description:
All Things AI (Live)
In this session of *Newsweek’s* “AI Impact Forum,” **Dr. Ranjit Tinaikar** speaks with **Duncan Angove**, chief executive officer of Blue Yonder, about bringing enterprise AI into warehouses, factories, transportation networks and other environments where digital decisions have immediate real-world consequences.
Angove describes supply chain as a “messy frontier” for AI, shaped by constant movement, unpredictable edge cases and institutional knowledge built through years of human experience. The conversation will examine how companies can combine general-purpose AI with specialized models designed for specific operational tasks, while preserving the expertise that distinguishes how their businesses run.
Tinaikar and Angove will also explore what increasingly autonomous systems could mean for the economics of enterprise technology. That includes whether companies begin focusing less on software seats or AI consumption and more on measurable outcomes such as moving goods faster, improving productivity and lowering operating costs.
The discussion will extend to the people operating alongside these systems: how companies build trust, manage adoption and use AI to augment the judgment and experience required in complex frontline work.

Designed for CEOs, supply chain and operations leaders, technology executives and other senior decision-makers, the session will offer a practical look at how AI is changing the systems and decisions behind the movement of goods through the global economy.

title: Science Café: Decoding the Lives of Sri Lanka’s Elephants
location: Downtown Raleigh, 11 West Jones Street, Raleigh, NC, 27601, United States
description:
Grab a bite from the Daily Planet Café and join host Chris Smith for our monthly Science Café. Gather with other curious minds for an informal presentation and conversation about current science topics with guest experts. The Daily Planet Café is open 5–8pm with a full menu during the Science Café. 
Join us in-person or watch the livestream on YouTube. 
Tonight’s Topic 
In Sri Lanka’s North Central Province, expanding agriculture is increasing overlap between human settlements and elephant habitat. Elephants that forage on farm crops face retaliation from farmers protecting their livelihoods, making Human-Elephant Conflict (HEC) one of the region’s most pressing conservation challenges. Yet not all elephants engage in crop raiding, and little is known about the characteristics that influence the likelihood of crop raiding. This talk presents ongoing research examining behavioral and genetic variation within the North Central Province’s elephant population to identify factors associated with conflict. This work aims to inform evidence-based conservation strategies and support coexistence between local communities and elephants. 
Tonight’s Expert 
Julia Brzezicki is a second year PhD student in the Department of Biological Sciences at North Carolina State University under the supervision of Dr. Bruce A. Schulte. She is from the Buffalo, New York region, and she earned her BSc in biology from SUNY Geneseo and her MSc in biology from Western Kentucky University where her thesis focused on the behavioral variation of Asian elephants in Sri Lanka. Julia is a recipient of a Fulbright award to support her continued research and collaborations in Sri Lanka. She has been studying elephants for four years and she seeks to integrate ecological, behavioral, and genetic research to support the development of local sustainable elephant conservation initiatives in Sri Lanka.

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).
